The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be an
invertible linear map ([[def-linear-map]]). Then:

1. $T[E]$ is a Borel set for every Borel set $E$, and $T$ carries open sets to
   open sets;
2. there is a strictly positive real $c(T)$, namely
   $c(T) = \lambda_n\big(T[(0,1]^n]\big)$, with
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; c(T)\,\lambda_n(E) \qquad \text{for every } E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n);$$
3. $c(S \circ T) = c(S)\,c(T)$ for invertible linear $S$ and $T$, and
   $c(\mathrm{id}) = 1$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{int}W$ and $r>0$ with the open ball $B(x_0,r)\subseteq W$. For $0<t<1$ put $W_t=x_0+(1-t)(W-x_0)$. If $w\in W$ and $\|z\|<tr$, then $x_0+z/t\in B(x_0,r)\subseteq W$ and $$(1-t)w+t(x_0+z/t)=(1-t)w+tx_0+z\in W$$ by convexity; thus every point of $W_t$ has an open ball of radius $tr$ contained in $W$, so $W_t\subseteq\operatorname{int}W$.

If $0<t'<t<1$, put $w'=\frac{1-t}{1-t'}w+\frac{t-t'}{1-t'}x_0$. The two coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so $w'\in W$ by convexity, and $$x_0+(1-t)(w-x_0)=x_0+(1-t')(w'-x_0).$$ Thus $W_t\subseteq W_{t'}$. Moreover, every $y\in\operatorname{int}W$ lies in some $W_t$: for $y\ne x_0$, choose $s>0$ small enough that $w=x_0+(1+s)(y-x_0)\in W$, and then $y=x_0+(1-t)(w-x_0)$ for $t=s/(1+s)$; $x_0$ lies in every $W_t$. Hence for any sequence $t_n\downarrow0$, $W_{t_n}\uparrow\operatorname{int}W$.

By [F2] and [F3], $|W_{t_n}|=(1-t_n)^d|W|$ and the sets increase to $\operatorname{int}W$, so [F3] gives $|\operatorname{int}W|=|W|$. Thus the compact boundary $\partial W=W\setminus\operatorname{int}W$ is a null set. Since $W$ contains a nonempty open ball and is bounded, [F1] gives $0<|W|<\infty$.

Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $t>0$ so that $|W|-|W_t|=(1-(1-t)^d)|W|<\epsilon$. Choose a grid of half-open cubes of side $\delta< tr/\sqrt d$. Each cube that intersects $W_t$ is contained in $W$, because its points lie within distance at most $\sqrt d\delta<tr$ of a point whose radius-$tr$ ball lies in $W$. Only finitely many grid cubes intersect bounded $W_t$; their union $R$ is disjoint, finite, contains $W_t$, and is contained in $W$. Therefore $|W\setminus R|\le |W\setminus W_t|<\epsilon$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ and choose $R\subseteq W$ as in step 4.1, a finite union of disjoint rectangles. Translation invariance and the symmetric-difference inclusion give $$|(W+h)\triangle W|\le2|W\setminus R|+|(R+h)\triangle R|.$$ For each half-open rectangle, its overlap with a translate by $h$ has volume tending to the rectangle's volume as $h\to0$, by the box-volume formula; the same limit holds for their finite union. Thus $\limsup_{h\to0}|(W+h)\triangle W|\le2\epsilon$, and arbitrariness of $\epsilon$ gives convergence to zero.
For $a>0$, [F2] gives $|aW|=a^d|W|$ and $|(aW+x)\triangle aW|=a^d|(W+x/a)\triangle W|$. Dividing and applying step 5.1 with $h=x/a\to0$ proves the asserted boundary ratio.

Steps 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1 prove positive finite volume, the finite inner rectangle approximation, dilation scaling, and the translated-boundary limit. Countable Choice is used only through [F1]–[F2]; no AC or DC is used.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu$ be a measure on
$\big(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)\big)$ ([[def-measure]]) such that
$\mu(E+h) = \mu(E)$ for every Borel set $E$ and every $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and
$\mu\big((0,1]^n\big) = 1$. Then

$$\mu(E) \;=\; \lambda_n(E) \qquad \text{for every } E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n).$$

The hypothesis is meaningful because a translate of a Borel set is Borel, and it
is satisfied by the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, so
the theorem says that measure is the only one satisfying it. Finiteness on
bounded sets is a consequence of the normalisation, not a further hypothesis.

derivations.claim: Fix a coordinate $i$ and either face $F$ of $[0,1]^d$ in that coordinate. For each integer $n\ge1$, translate the lower face by $j/(n+1)e_i$, or the upper face by $-j/(n+1)e_i$, for $j=1,\ldots,n$. These $n$ translates are pairwise disjoint compact subsets of $[0,1]^d$, each has measure $m(F)$ by translation invariance, and $m([0,1]^d)<\infty$ by local finiteness. Hence $n m(F)\le m([0,1]^d)$ for every $n$, which forces $m(F)=0$. The boundary of $[0,1]^d$ is a finite union of such faces.
The symmetric difference of $Q$ and $(0,1]^d$ is contained in that boundary, so [F1] and step 1.1 give $m(Q)=m((0,1]^d)=c$.

If $c=0$, the integer translates $Q+k$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, are a countable disjoint partition of $\mathbb R^d$. Translation invariance gives $m(Q+k)=0$ for every $k$, and countable additivity gives $m(\mathbb R^d)=0$. Monotonicity then gives $m(B)=0$ for every Borel $B$.
If $c>0$, $m/c$ is a translation-invariant Borel measure and, by step 2.1, $(m/c)((0,1]^d)=1$. Applying [F2] gives $m/c=\lambda_d$, hence $m(B)=c\lambda_d(B)$ for every Borel $B$.
The cases $c=0$ and $c>0$ exhaust the nonnegative value $m(Q)$, proving the statement. The proof uses Countable Choice only through [F2]; no stronger choice principle is used.

Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: First suppose $\mathbb E X_1=0$ and $|X_n|\le1$ almost surely for each $n$. Put $A_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j$ and $L=\limsup_n A_n$. Then $-1\le L\le1$, and for every fixed $p\ge1$ the averages $m^{-1}\sum_{j=p}^{p+m-1}X_j$ have the same limsup $L$: their difference from $A_m$ is at most $2(p-1)/m$, which tends to zero.

Fix $0<\epsilon<1/4$. For each $p\ge1$ let $T_p$ be the least positive integer $m$ for which $m^{-1}\sum_{j=p}^{p+m-1}X_j>L-\epsilon$. Such an $m$ exists by the definition of limsup; [F1] and shift invariance show that the $T_p$ all have the same distribution. Choose an integer $k$ so that $\mathbb P(T_1>k)<\epsilon$, and set $X_p^*=X_p+2\mathbf1_{\{T_p>k\}}$.

For every $p$, $X_p^*\ge-1$ and $\mathbb E X_p^*=2\mathbb P(T_1>k)<2\epsilon$. Define $T_p^*$ as the first $m\ge1$ for which the average of $X_p^*,\ldots,X_{p+m-1}^*$ exceeds $L-\epsilon$. If $T_p\le k$, the same average of the larger sequence $X_j^*$ at length $T_p$ exceeds $L-\epsilon$; if $T_p>k$, then $X_p^*=X_p+2\ge1>L-\epsilon$. Thus $1\le T_p^*\le k$ in either case.

Starting from $M_0=0$, recursively set $M_{q+1}=M_q+T^*_{M_q+1}$. Each increment is between $1$ and $k$, and the average of $X_j^*$ on each block $(M_q,M_{q+1}]$ exceeds $L-\epsilon$. Therefore $S^*_{M_q}:=\sum_{j=1}^{M_q}X_j^*>(L-\epsilon)M_q$.

For $n\ge k$, take the last $M_q\le n$; then $0\le n-M_q<k$. The remaining terms are at least $-1$, so $S_n^*>S_{M_q}^*-k>(L-\epsilon)M_q-k\ge(L-\epsilon)n-2k$, using $L-\epsilon\le1$. Hence $n^{-1}S_n^*>L-\epsilon-2k/n$.

Stationarity gives $\mathbb E[n^{-1}S_n^*]=\mathbb E X_1^*<2\epsilon$. Taking expectations in step 5.1 and then letting $n\to\infty$ gives $\mathbb E L\le3\epsilon$. Since this holds for every such $\epsilon$, $\mathbb E L\le0$. Applying the same argument to $(-X_n)$ shows $\mathbb E[\liminf_n A_n]\ge0$. The bounded nonnegative difference $\limsup_nA_n-\liminf_nA_n$ therefore has expectation at most zero, so it vanishes almost surely. Thus $A_n$ converges almost surely; [F2] gives convergence in $L^1$.

If instead $|X_n|\le C<\infty$ without centering, the case $C=0$ is immediate; for $C>0$ apply the preceding result to $(X_n-\mathbb E X_1)/(2C)$, whose terms are centered and have absolute value at most $1$. Rescaling and adding $\mathbb E X_1$ proves the bounded case.

Suppose $X_n\ge0$ and is integrable but not necessarily bounded. For $r\ge1$ set $X_{n,r}=X_n\wedge r$ and $A_{n,r}=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nX_{j,r}$. Define the limit canonically by $Y_r:=\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_{n,r}$; it is measurable by [F1]. By step 7.1, the averages converge almost surely and in $L^1$ to this integrable $Y_r$. On the common probability-one event for these countably many convergences, $Y_r\le Y_{r+1}$; also $Y_r\ge0$ and $\mathbb E Y_r=\mathbb E X_{1,r}$.

Let $Y=\lim_{r\to\infty}Y_r$. By [F3], $Y$ is integrable and $\mathbb E Y=\mathbb E X_1$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $r$ with $\mathbb E(X_1-X_{1,r})<\epsilon$; then also $\mathbb E(Y-Y_r)<\epsilon$. For this fixed $r$, stationarity and nonnegativity give $\mathbb E|A_n-A_{n,r}|=\mathbb E(X_1-X_{1,r})<\epsilon$, while $\mathbb E|A_{n,r}-Y_r|\to0$. The triangle inequality proves $\limsup_n\mathbb E|A_n-Y|\le2\epsilon$, and arbitrariness of $\epsilon$ gives $L^1$ convergence.

For a signed integrable stationary sequence, apply the nonnegative case in steps 8.1–9.1 separately to $X_n^+=\max(X_n,0)$ and $X_n^-=\max(-X_n,0)$. Both are stationary nonnegative integrable sequences, and subtracting their $L^1$ limits gives an integrable $L^1$ limit for the averages of $X_n$. The entire argument used no choice principle.

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Assume $\eta$ is a stationary point process as in [[def-stationary-point-process-and-intensity]]. It is **locally square integrable** if $\mathbb E[\eta(K)^2]<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. For a realized counting measure $\mu=\sum_{i\in J}\delta_{X_i}$, with occurrences indexed separately even when locations coincide, as allowed by [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]], define its second factorial measure on Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$ by

$$\mu^{(2)}(C):=\sum_{i,j\in J,\ i\ne j}\mathbf1_C(X_i,X_j).$$

The **second factorial moment measure** is $\alpha^{(2)}(C):=\mathbb E[\eta^{(2)}(C)]$. With $Q=[0,1)^d$, the **reduced second factorial moment measure** is

$$\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D):=\mathbb E\sum_{i,j\in J,\ i\ne j}\mathbf1_Q(X_i)\mathbf1_D(X_j-X_i),\qquad D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}.$$

The local theorem [[thm-second-factorial-and-reduced-measures-are-locally-finite]] proves measurability and local finiteness under local square integrability. Occurrence indices, rather than distinct locations, are essential when multiplicities are present.

**Axiom convention.** AC and Countable Choice are carried by the transitive point-process supplier dependencies; the occurrence-indexed formulas themselves make no selections.

$$(\theta_x\mu)(B):=\mu(B+x).$$

**Axiom convention.** The point-process supplier used for this definition has transitive dependencies on AC and Countable Choice; the recentering formula itself makes no selections.

Recentering $\theta_x$ is as in [[def-spatial-recentering-action]]. The process is **stationary** if $\theta_x\eta$ has law $P_\eta$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$.

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

derivations.claim: For every Borel $B$, $u\mapsto\eta_u(B)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mathbf1_B(k+u)$ is measurable as a countable sum of Borel functions; every compact set meets only finitely many points of each $\eta_u$, so this is a locally finite random counting measure. For fixed $x$, put $t=x-\lfloor x\rfloor\in[0,1)$. The map $u\mapsto\{u-x\}$ is a translation on each of $[0,t)$ and $[t,1)$, with the two image intervals partitioning $[0,1)$; by [F2] it preserves uniform probability. Reindexing $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives $\theta_x\eta_u=\eta_{\{u-x\}}$, so the process is stationary. Since exactly one $k+u$ lies in $Q=[0,1)$ for every $u\in[0,1)$, $\eta_U(Q)=1$ and $\rho=1$.

For every compact $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, choose an integer $m\ge1$ with $C\subseteq[-m,m]$. If $u\in[0,1)$ and $k+u\in C$, then $-m-1\le k\le m$, so $\eta_u(C)\le2m+2$ uniformly in $u$. Consequently $\mathbb E[\eta_U(C)^2]\le(2m+2)^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E[(2\eta_U)(C)^2]\le4(2m+2)^2<\infty$. Both lattice processes satisfy the local square-integrability premise in the second-order and K definitions.

For every configuration event $A$, the unit-cube Palm construction in [F3] gives $$P^0(A)=\mathbb E\int_Q\mathbf1_A(\theta_x\eta_U)\eta_U(dx).$$ There is exactly one occurrence $x=U$ in $Q$, and $\theta_U\eta_U=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\delta_k=:\Lambda$. Therefore $P^0=\delta_\Lambda$. In particular, using the uncentered configuration in the indicator $\mathbf1_{\{\mu(\{0\})>0\}}$ would give $0$ on the left Campbell sum almost surely, whereas the Palm-side value is $1$; this is why recentering cannot be dropped.

For each selected lattice occurrence $X_i=k+U\in Q$, the displacements to all other occurrences are $\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Hence [F4] gives $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(D)=\#(D\cap(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}))$ for bounded Borel $D$. In particular $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{1\})=1$ while $|\{1\}|=0$, so no measurable density $g$ can satisfy [F5].

Now put $\widetilde\eta_U=2\eta_U$, so every lattice site has two occurrence indices and $\widetilde\rho=2$. A selected occurrence has one other occurrence at the same site, so $\alpha^{(2)}_{\rm red}(\{0\})=2$. Equivalently, $P^0$ is concentrated on $2\Lambda$, and $\mu(\{0\})=2$, so [F6] gives $2=\widetilde\rho\mathbb E^0[(\mu-\delta_0)(\{0\})]=2\cdot1$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
